title: ITD 256 Extra Practice
description: Everything outside the core review — broader coverage of the same topics, for when you want more reps.

sections.name: Database Concepts, File Systems & Data Models

questions.question: "Raw facts, such as a telephone number or a birth date, that have little meaning unless organized in some logical manner" is the definition of:
questions.explanation: That's data. Information is what you get after data is processed and given context.

questions.question: A character or group of characters, alpha or numeric, that has a specific meaning is called a ______.
questions.explanation: A field — known as an attribute once you're talking in database terms.

questions.question: In a DBMS, a collection of related records is called a table. In a file-based system, the same collection is called a:
questions.explanation: Same definition, different name: file outside a DBMS, table inside one.

questions.question: XML — the usual example of semistructured data — stands for Extensible ______ Language.
questions.explanation: Extensible Markup Language. It represents data elements in a textual format.

questions.question: Databases can also be classified by location. Match each type to its description.

pairs.right: Data is located at a single site
Data is spread across several different sites
Created and maintained with cloud services that provide defined performance measures

questions.explanation: Location-based classification: one site, many sites, or a cloud provider's infrastructure.

questions.question: A database that stores historical data and business metrics used exclusively for tactical or strategic decision making is a(n):
questions.explanation: Analytical databases support decision making. Transactional (operational) databases support day-to-day operations.

questions.question: Match each decision-support term to what it actually is.

pairs.right: Stores data in a format optimized for decision support
Tools that retrieve, process and model data from a data warehouse
Capturing and processing business data to generate information supporting decisions

questions.explanation: OLAP stands for online analytical processing — the tooling layer that sits over the warehouse.

questions.question: OLAP stands for online ______ processing.
questions.explanation: Online analytical processing — the tools used to retrieve, process and model data from a data warehouse.

questions.question: Modern end-user productivity tools such as Microsoft Excel are a kind of "file system redux" — they reintroduce file-system problems.
questions.explanation: Spreadsheets are a file system redux: convenient, but they bring back redundancy and inconsistency.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a problem of file systems?
options: Difficulty getting quick answers to ad hoc queries
questions.explanation: File systems don't enforce referential integrity at all — that's one of the things a DBMS adds.

questions.question: Match each dependence/independence term to its meaning.

pairs.right: Access to a file depends on its own structure, so programs must change when the structure does
The file structure can change without affecting the application's ability to access the data
Data access changes when data storage characteristics change
Storage characteristics can change without affecting the program's ability to access data

questions.explanation: Structural is about the shape of the file; data is about how it's physically stored. In both cases, independence is the goal.

questions.question: The physical format — how data is actually stored on hardware — should be hidden completely from the end user.
questions.explanation: Physical storage should be hidden completely and of no concern to the user.

questions.question: Compared with a file system, a database system provides:
options: Less data independence, but faster raw file access
More data independence, more robust organization, and better control of data access
Identical data independence, with only a different user interface
questions.explanation: The three advantages are exactly these: more data independence, more robust organization, better control of data access.

questions.question: Scattered, duplicated data locations are described with the phrase:
questions.explanation: Islands of information — the same data kept in several disconnected places.

questions.question: Which is NOT listed as a possible result of uncontrolled data redundancy?
questions.explanation: Poor security, inconsistency, data-entry errors, integrity problems and anomalies are the listed consequences. Performance is not among them.

questions.question: Anomalies develop when not all of the required changes in redundant data are made ______.
questions.explanation: If redundant copies are only partly updated, the data disagrees with itself — that's an anomaly.

questions.question: A community centre keeps instructor phone numbers in every row of its CLASS_SESSION table. An instructor changes number, but only some rows get edited. Which anomaly is this?
questions.explanation: An update anomaly: redundant copies were only partly changed, so the table now holds two different numbers for one instructor.

questions.question: The same centre cannot record a newly hired instructor until that instructor is assigned to a class, because instructor details live only in CLASS_SESSION. Which anomaly is this?
questions.explanation: An insertion anomaly: you can't add one fact without also having an unrelated one.

questions.question: Deleting the last class an instructor taught also erases that instructor's phone number entirely. Which anomaly is this?
questions.explanation: A deletion anomaly: removing one fact takes an unrelated fact down with it.

questions.question: A database system is an organization of five components. Match each to its role.

pairs.right: The physical devices the system runs on
The operating system, the DBMS, and application programs
Administrators, designers, programmers and end users
The rules and instructions governing how the system is used
The raw facts stored in the database itself

questions.explanation: Hardware, software, people, procedures and data — all five together make up the database system environment.

questions.question: Match each DBMS function to what it does.

pairs.right: Enforces user security and data privacy
Lets many users work concurrently without compromising integrity
Enables recovery of the database after a failure
Minimizes redundancy and maximizes consistency
Part of storage management; ensures efficient performance

questions.explanation: These are the standard DBMS functions. Notice that integrity management is defined in terms of redundancy and consistency.

questions.question: Which DBMS function makes it possible for many users to work in the database at once without corrupting it?
questions.explanation: Multiuser access control uses algorithms to ensure concurrent access without compromising integrity.

questions.question: In a query language, who decides HOW the result is produced?
options: The user, by writing the access path step by step
The system — the user specifies only what result they want
The application programmer, in the host language
questions.explanation: That's the defining property: users specify what they want, and the system determines how to produce it. This is why SQL is called nonprocedural.

questions.question: Every DBMS vendor implements SQL identically, so a query written for one product always runs unchanged on another.
questions.explanation: SQL is supported by nearly all vendors, but with slight variations — dialects differ, especially around dates and built-in functions.

questions.question: A simple representation of complex real-world data structures, useful for supporting a specific problem domain, is called a data ______.
questions.explanation: A data model. Data modeling is the act of creating one for a determined problem domain.

questions.question: To determine the type of a relationship between entities A and B, you ask:
options: Only how many instances of B relate to one instance of A
How many instances of B relate to one A, AND how many instances of A relate to one B
Whether A or B was created first
questions.explanation: Both directions. Answering only one gives you half the cardinality and usually the wrong diagram.

questions.question: Match each relationship type to the two notations used for it.

pairs.right: M:N or *..*

questions.explanation: The colon form and the dotted UML-style form mean the same thing.

questions.question: Which naming convention is recommended for entity names?
options: Short codes that only the DBA needs to understand
Descriptive of the business environment, using terminology familiar to users
Always the plural of the attribute name
Sequential names such as TABLE1, TABLE2
questions.explanation: Good names are descriptive, match the business environment, and use terminology users already know — which promotes self-documentation.

questions.question: Match each formal relational term to its everyday equivalent.

pairs.right: Table
Row
Column

questions.explanation: Relation/tuple/attribute is the formal vocabulary; table/row/column is what you'll actually say out loud.

questions.question: An entity ______, also called an entity occurrence, corresponds to a row in a relational table.
questions.explanation: Entity instance (or entity occurrence) = one row.

questions.question: ______ is the term used to label relationship types on an ERD (1:1, 1:M, M:N).
questions.explanation: Connectivity labels the relationship type. Cardinality expresses the specific numbers involved.

questions.question: Match each object-oriented term to its relational-model analogue.

pairs.right: Record
Entity or table
A property of an object

questions.explanation: An object is analogous to a record; a class is analogous to an entity/table — a class is a template from which individual objects are created.

questions.question: In the object-oriented data model, what distinguishes an object from a plain record?
options: An object contains data and relationships along with the operations to perform on that data
An object cannot be stored persistently
questions.explanation: The object holds data, relationships and its own operations together in a single structure.

questions.question: In an object-oriented class hierarchy, what does inheritance do?
options: Lets an object take on the methods and attributes of its parent classes
Copies every row from the parent table
Forces every class to have two parents
Removes attributes from the child class
questions.explanation: The hierarchy resembles an upside-down tree — each class has only one parent — and an object inherits the methods and attributes of its parent classes.

questions.question: In an object-oriented class hierarchy, each class may have many parent classes.
questions.explanation: The hierarchy resembles an upside-down tree in which each class has only one parent.

questions.question: Ordered from more abstract to less abstract, the levels of data modeling run:
options: Chen notation → Crow's Foot notation → DDL SQL
questions.explanation: Chen is the most abstract, Crow's Foot sits in the middle, and DDL SQL is the least abstract — it's the actual implementation.

questions.question: A data dictionary stores the definitions of data elements and their relationships.
questions.explanation: That's the definition given for the data dictionary, and data dictionary management is a core DBMS function.

questions.question: Which job title covers the design and implementation of conceptual, logical AND physical database environments?
questions.explanation: The Database Architect covers all three levels of the environment.

questions.question: What two jobs do keys do?
options: Speed up sorting, and compress storage
Ensure each row is uniquely identifiable, and establish relationships among tables
Encrypt sensitive columns, and audit access
Replace the need for a data dictionary
questions.explanation: Unique identification plus relationships between tables (and therefore data integrity).

questions.question: Match each type of key to its definition.

pairs.right: The attribute or combination that uniquely identifies a row
A key composed of more than one attribute
Any key that can uniquely identify a row
A minimal superkey — nothing can be removed from it
The primary key of one table placed in another to create a common attribute
A key used strictly for data retrieval purposes

questions.explanation: Note the relationship: every candidate key is a superkey, but a superkey is only a candidate key if it's minimal.

questions.question: A candidate key is a ______ superkey — one from which no attribute can be removed and still identify a row.
questions.explanation: Minimal. Add an extra column to a candidate key and you still have a superkey, but no longer a candidate key.

questions.question: A SHIFT_LOG table has columns (badge_no, shift_date, start_time, end_time, post_name). A worker can appear only once per date. Which is a superkey but NOT a candidate key?
questions.explanation: (badge_no, shift_date) already identifies a row, so adding post_name still identifies it — a superkey — but it is no longer minimal, so it is not a candidate key.

questions.question: An attribute that is part of a key is called a ______ attribute.
questions.explanation: A key attribute. Attributes that are not part of any candidate key are called nonprime (or non-key) attributes.

questions.question: Which is NOT a reason to use a surrogate primary key?
options: There is no natural key suitable as a primary key
The natural primary key would be a composite key with multiple data types
The natural primary key is too long to be usable
The table has fewer than one thousand rows
questions.explanation: Table size isn't a reason. The three listed reasons are: no suitable natural key, an awkward multi-type composite, or a key that's simply too long.

questions.question: A tool library identifies each borrower by an auto-numbered patron_id rather than by their email address. patron_id is a:
questions.explanation: It's made up by the system rather than drawn from the real world, so it's a surrogate key.

questions.question: The condition in which each row in a table has its own unique identity is called ______ integrity.
questions.explanation: Entity integrity: all primary key values are unique, and no part of a primary key may be null.

questions.question: Under referential integrity, a foreign key column may:
options: Contain any value at all, checked only by the application
Contain either a null, or a value that matches a primary key in the related table
Never contain a null under any circumstances
Contain only values that do not appear in the related table
questions.explanation: Null is allowed (the relationship may simply be optional); an invalid, non-matching value is not.

questions.question: A standard example of referential integrity: a customer might not yet have an assigned sales representative — but it is impossible to have an INVALID one. What does the null represent there?
options: A data-entry error that must be corrected
An optional relationship that has not been filled in yet
questions.explanation: The null marks an optional participation — no representative assigned yet. Referential integrity blocks invalid values, not missing ones.

questions.question: Enforcing referential integrity makes it impossible to delete a row whose primary key has mandatory matching foreign key values in another table.
questions.explanation: Exactly — that's why you delete children before parents. The practice database in the SQL playground will refuse such a delete if you try it.

questions.question: Which of these violates ENTITY integrity rather than referential integrity?
options: A loan row points at a patron_id that does not exist
Two rows in the patron table share patron_id 14
A branch row has a null locality_id where the relationship is optional
A foreign key column is indexed
questions.explanation: Duplicate primary key values break entity integrity. A dangling foreign key breaks referential integrity.

questions.question: Which is NOT one of the three things a null can mean?
options: A known but missing attribute value
questions.explanation: Zero is a real value. Null is the absence of a value — which is why it needs IS NULL rather than = 0.

questions.question: Which relationship type is the norm for relational databases?
questions.explanation: 1:M is the most common type in relational databases.

questions.question: The bridge table in an M:N relationship goes by several names. Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: The connecting table created to resolve an M:N relationship
Another name for that same connecting table
A third name for it, emphasising that it records an association

questions.explanation: Composite, bridge and associative all name the same thing. It includes the primary keys of the tables being linked, as foreign keys.

questions.question: In a 1:M relationship, where does the foreign key go?
options: In the table on the "one" side
In the table on the "many" side
questions.explanation: The foreign key always goes on the many side, referencing the primary key on the one side.

questions.question: Although relational tables are independent of one another, they can be linked through common attributes — that is, foreign keys.
questions.explanation: Independent tables, linked by common attributes — that is the whole idea of the relational model.

questions.question: What is the basic building block of a relational database?
questions.explanation: Tables are the basic building blocks, and keys are central to using them.

questions.question: A key that is used strictly for data retrieval purposes — not to enforce uniqueness or relationships — is called a ______ key.
questions.explanation: A secondary key exists to make retrieval convenient, e.g. looking customers up by surname.

questions.question: A SEAT_BOOKING table has (performance_id, seat_code, patron_id, price_paid), where performance_id + seat_code together identify a booking. What kind of key is (performance_id, seat_code)?
questions.explanation: One key made of more than one attribute is a composite key; here it's the primary key, so a composite primary key.

questions.question:
A SEAT_BOOKING table has (performance_id, seat_code, patron_id, price_paid), where performance_id + seat_code together identify a booking.

patron_id refers to the primary key of a PATRON table. patron_id is therefore:
options: Part of the composite primary key
questions.explanation: The primary key of one table placed in another is a foreign key — the common attribute that links them.

questions.question: A foreign key and the primary key it references must have the same column name.
questions.explanation: They usually do — which is what makes NATURAL JOIN and JOIN USING convenient — but it isn't required. When the names differ, join with JOIN ... ON.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of duplicate column names across two joined tables?
options: The existence of a foreign key
questions.explanation: The foreign key deliberately repeats the parent's primary key name, so joining the two tables produces two columns with that name.

questions.question: "In ERM, an M:N relationship is valid at the conceptual level." What must happen before it becomes a logical/physical design?
options: Nothing — it can be implemented directly
It must be resolved into a bridge table, giving two 1:M relationships
One of the two entities must be deleted
It must be converted into a 1:1 relationship
questions.explanation: Conceptually M:N is fine; logically you need the bridge table.

questions.question: ______ describes the relationship classification — 1:1, 1:M or M:N — on an ERD.
questions.explanation: Connectivity and cardinality are used together for this: connectivity labels the type, cardinality expresses the numbers.

questions.question: Database designers, however effective, are often forced to make design compromises.
questions.explanation: The clean textbook answer and the practical answer sometimes differ; real designs involve trade-offs.

questions.question: A tool library wants to record that each UNIT (a physical copy) belongs to exactly one BRANCH, while a BRANCH holds many UNITs. Which design is correct?
options: A bridge table between UNIT and BRANCH
questions.explanation: 1:M with UNIT on the many side, so the foreign key branch_id lives in UNIT. No bridge table is needed unless a unit could belong to several branches at once.

questions.question: A catalogue GADGET can belong to several GROUPs (Plumbing, Measuring…), and each GROUP contains many GADGETs. What does the design need?
options: A bridge entity holding gadget_id and group_id as foreign keys
Nothing — store the group names in a text column
questions.explanation: That's M:N, so it needs a bridge entity. This is exactly the gadget_group_map table in the practice database.

questions.question: In your own words, explain the difference between entity integrity and referential integrity, and give one example of a violation of each.
questions.modelAnswer:
Entity integrity concerns the primary key of a row: every primary key value must be unique and no part of it may be null, so each row has its own identity. A violation would be two rows in PATRON sharing patron_id 14, or a row with a null patron_id.

Referential integrity concerns a foreign key: it must either be null or match an existing primary key value in the related table. A violation would be a CHECKOUT row whose patron_id is 9999 when no such patron exists.
rubric: Said entity integrity is about the primary key being unique and not null
Said referential integrity is about a foreign key matching an existing primary key (or being null)
Gave a concrete violation of entity integrity (duplicate or null PK)
Gave a concrete violation of referential integrity (a foreign key pointing at a row that doesn't exist)
questions.explanation: The short version: entity integrity looks inward at the row's own identity; referential integrity looks outward at the row it points to.

questions.question: A club tracks MEMBERs and the EVENTs they attend. A member may attend many events, and an event may be attended by many members. Describe the tables you would create, and name the key in each.
questions.modelAnswer:
Three tables.

MEMBER — primary key member_id, plus member attributes (name, contact details).
EVENT — primary key event_id, plus event attributes (title, date, venue).
ATTENDANCE (the bridge/composite entity) — member_id and event_id, each a foreign key to its parent table, and together the composite primary key. Any attribute that describes the pairing rather than the member or the event alone — for example checked_in_at — also belongs here.

The M:N is now two 1:M relationships: one MEMBER has many ATTENDANCE rows, and one EVENT has many ATTENDANCE rows.
rubric: Created three tables, not two
Named a bridge/composite/associative table between MEMBER and EVENT
Said the bridge holds both member_id and event_id as foreign keys
Said those two together form the composite primary key of the bridge
questions.explanation: Recognising "many ... many" in a business rule and reaching straight for a third table is the single most reliable ERD reflex to build.

questions.question: SQL functions fall into four categories. Match each abbreviation to what it does.

pairs.right: Data definition — creates and alters the structures themselves
Data manipulation — reads and changes the rows
Transaction control — COMMIT and ROLLBACK
Data control — grants and revokes access rights

questions.explanation: SQL has essentially two sets of commands — DDL and DML — with TCL and DCL alongside them.

questions.question: SQL is a nonprocedural language with a basic command vocabulary of:
questions.explanation: Under 100 words — one reason SQL is described as relatively easy to learn.

questions.question: Match each column constraint to what it enforces.

pairs.right: The column may not be left empty
The column may not contain duplicate values
Defines the table's unique row identifier
Ties the column to a primary key in another table
Supplies a value when none is given
Validates the data placed in the attribute

questions.explanation: These are the constraint options available on CREATE TABLE.

questions.question: Which command permanently deletes an entire database, including all of its tables?
questions.explanation: DROP DATABASE. DELETE is DML and removes rows; DROP is DDL and removes structures.

questions.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
options: WHERE filters individual rows; HAVING filters the groups produced by GROUP BY
WHERE works only on numbers; HAVING works only on text
questions.explanation: WHERE filters rows on the way in, HAVING filters groups on the way out. That is why an aggregate like count(*) can appear in HAVING but not in WHERE.

questions.question: Which clause would you use to keep only the groups whose total exceeds 500?
questions.explanation: Aggregates belong in HAVING, because the groups don't exist yet when WHERE runs.

questions.question: In `SELECT * FROM payment;` what does the asterisk do?
options: Repeats the query for every table
Acts as a wildcard standing in for every column
Limits the result to the first row
questions.explanation: The asterisk is a wildcard: a symbol used as a substitute for other characters or commands. Here it means every column.

questions.question: Match each comparison operator to its meaning.

pairs.right: Equal to
Less than
Greater than or equal to
Not equal to

questions.explanation: SQL accepts both <> and != for "not equal".

questions.question: Why does `WHERE returned_on = NULL` never match anything?
options: Because NULL must be written in lowercase
Because null is the absence of a value, so equality can't be tested — you need IS NULL
Because the column has to be indexed first
questions.explanation: Null means "no value here", so comparing it with = yields neither true nor false. IS NULL is the test.

questions.question: Old-style joins — writing `WHERE table1.pk = table2.fk` instead of a JOIN clause — are generally not recommended because they:
options: Make complex queries harder to maintain and are susceptible to undetected errors
Are not supported by any modern DBMS
Cannot be used with WHERE at all
questions.explanation: They still work, but the join condition gets mixed in with the row filters, which is easy to get wrong without noticing.

questions.question: Match each join to what it returns.

pairs.right: Only the rows from both tables that match on the common value
The matched rows, plus unmatched rows from one table or the other
Rows matching on identically named columns, with duplicate columns eliminated
A join of a table to itself

questions.explanation: Recursive joins are unary; every other join is binary.

questions.question: How does a NATURAL JOIN decide which columns to join on?
options: By the order the columns are declared
By finding attributes with identical names and compatible data types in both tables
By using the first column of each table
By reading the foreign key constraints only
questions.explanation: It looks for identically named, type-compatible columns. If there are none, it returns the relational product of the tables — usually not what you wanted.

questions.question: A natural join eliminates the duplicate common column from its result.
questions.explanation: It returns rows with matching values in the matching columns and eliminates the duplicate column.

questions.question: When would you use JOIN … ON rather than JOIN … USING?
options: When the tables have no common attribute names
When you want a faster query
When there are more than two tables
When the join column is a primary key
questions.explanation: JOIN USING needs a column of the same name in both tables. JOIN ON lets you spell out any join condition, so it handles differing names.

questions.question: The ANSI standard defines three types of outer join. They are:
questions.explanation: Left, right and full outer joins.

questions.question: What is the practical benefit of giving a table an alias in a query?
options: It identifies the source table for each column and makes the query more maintainable
It is required by ANSI SQL for every query
questions.explanation: An alias identifies which table data came from and keeps long queries readable — and it is essential for a self-join.

questions.question: An aggregate query takes a collection of rows and reduces it to a single row.
questions.explanation: That is the definition of an aggregate query. Add GROUP BY and you get one row per group instead.

questions.question: Which command restores the database to its previous condition, undoing uncommitted changes?
questions.explanation: ROLLBACK. COMMIT is its counterpart — it saves the changes.

questions.question: The ______ command saves table changes permanently.
questions.explanation: COMMIT [WORK]. Until you commit, ROLLBACK can still undo the work.

questions.question: Which INSERT form adds many rows at once by drawing them from another table?
options: INSERT INTO target [(columns)] SELECT columns FROM source
INSERT MANY INTO target FROM source
questions.explanation: INSERT with a SELECT subquery uses another table as the source of the rows.

questions.question: Which list contains only basic ANSI data types?
options: NUMBER, NUMERIC, INTEGER, CHAR, VARCHAR, DATE
questions.explanation: NUMBER, NUMERIC, INTEGER, CHAR, VARCHAR and DATE — supported by all vendors, though in different ways.

questions.question: Because dates are stored as a number of days, it is possible to do date arithmetic inside a query.
questions.explanation: Yes — though comparison operators on dates are often more software-specific than other SQL procedures.

questions.question: In a cascading ORDER BY — last name, then first name, then middle initial — what does the second column control?
options: Nothing; only the first column has any effect
The order within groups of rows that tie on the first column
The order of the columns in the output
questions.explanation: Each subsequent column breaks ties left over from the previous one.

questions.question: Which keyword sorts an ORDER BY column from largest to smallest?
questions.explanation: DESC. ASC is ascending, and is the default when you write neither.

questions.question: List the gadget_title and replacement_cost of every gadget whose replacement_cost is greater than 500.
questions.explanation: WHERE adds a conditional restriction that limits the rows returned.

questions.question: List gadget_title and daily_fee for every gadget, most expensive first. Where two gadgets share the same daily_fee, order those by gadget_title.
questions.hint: A cascading ORDER BY: the second column breaks ties left by the first.
questions.explanation: DESC reverses the first sort key only; gadget_title stays ascending, which is the default.

questions.question: List every distinct power_source found in the gadget table, in alphabetical order.
questions.hint: The result should have no repeats.
questions.explanation: DISTINCT collapses the 45 rows down to the four values that actually occur.

questions.question: List the gadget_title of every gadget with the word SAW anywhere in the title.
questions.hint: LIKE with % on both sides. The % wildcard stands for any run of characters.
questions.explanation: LIKE '%SAW%' matches the word anywhere in the string. Note that it also catches Jigsaw and Chainsaw, where "saw" is inside a longer word.

questions.question: List maker_name and home_region for every maker based in Canada or Japan. Use a list operator rather than two OR conditions.
questions.hint: IN takes a parenthesised list of values.
questions.explanation: IN ('Canada','Japan') is shorthand for home_region='Canada' OR home_region='Japan'. Both are correct; IN is easier to read as the list grows.

questions.question: List checkout_id, unit_id and checked_out_on for every loan taken out between '2024-06-01' and '2024-08-31'. Use the BETWEEN…AND… keywords, and the YYYY-MM-DD format shown.
questions.hint: BETWEEN is inclusive at both ends.
questions.explanation: BETWEEN includes both endpoints, so a loan taken out on 1 June or 31 August counts.

questions.question: The returned_on column is empty for any tool still out on loan. List checkout_id, unit_id and due_on for every loan that has not yet come back.
questions.hint: "Empty" here means null — and null needs its own operator.
questions.explanation: IS NULL is the only way to find missing values; returned_on = NULL matches nothing at all.

questions.question: Find the total amount of every ledger_entry whose entry_kind is 'Late fee'. Return a single number.
questions.hint: An aggregate reduces many rows to one.
questions.explanation: SUM over the filtered rows. WHERE runs first, so only late fees are added up.

questions.question: How many separate loans has patron_id 34 taken out? Return a single count.
questions.explanation: count(*) counts the rows that survive the WHERE clause.

questions.question: How many loans were taken out in the month of July, across any year? Use the MONTH(date) function, which returns the numeric month of the date passed into it, against checked_out_on.
questions.hint: MONTH() turns a date into a number from 1 to 12.
questions.explanation: Applying a function to the column lets you filter on part of a date without knowing the year.

questions.question: Show patron_id and the number of loans for every patron who has taken out 8 or more. Alias the count as loans, and sort by loans descending, then by patron_id.
questions.hint: Group the rows, then filter the groups.
questions.solution:
SELECT patron_id, count(*) AS loans
FROM checkout
GROUP BY patron_id
HAVING count(*) >= 8
ORDER BY loans DESC, patron_id;
questions.explanation: GROUP BY makes one row per patron; HAVING then discards the groups that are too small. The same test in WHERE would be an error, because the groups don't exist yet.

questions.question: Every steward except the director reports to another steward, through supervisor_id. Show each steward's surname alongside their supervisor's surname, using the column names steward and reports_to. Sort by reports_to, then steward.
questions.hint: This is a recursive join — the table joined to itself. You'll need two different aliases for the same table.
questions.solution:
SELECT worker.surname AS steward,
       boss.surname   AS reports_to
FROM steward worker
INNER JOIN steward boss ON worker.supervisor_id = boss.steward_id
ORDER BY reports_to, steward;
questions.explanation: Aliases are what make a self-join possible: they give the query two distinguishable copies of one table. The director drops out because their supervisor_id is null and an inner join discards unmatched rows.

questions.question: Find the patrons who have never taken out a loan. Return patron_id and surname, sorted by patron_id.
questions.hint: An inner join can only show you patrons who DO appear in checkout. You need a join that keeps the unmatched rows — or a subquery.
questions.solution:
SELECT p.patron_id, p.surname
FROM patron p
LEFT JOIN checkout c ON c.patron_id = p.patron_id
WHERE c.checkout_id IS NULL
ORDER BY p.patron_id;
questions.explanation: The LEFT JOIN keeps every patron; those with no matching loan get nulls in the checkout columns, and testing one of those for IS NULL isolates them. `WHERE patron_id NOT IN (SELECT patron_id FROM checkout)` returns the same rows.

questions.question: Show power_source, how many gadgets use it (aliased as how_many), and the average daily_fee rounded to two decimal places (aliased as avg_fee). Sort by power_source.
questions.hint: Two aggregates over the same groups. round(value, 2) does the rounding.
questions.solution:
SELECT power_source,
       count(*) AS how_many,
       round(avg(daily_fee), 2) AS avg_fee
FROM gadget
GROUP BY power_source
ORDER BY power_source;
questions.explanation: Any column in the SELECT list that isn't aggregated has to appear in the GROUP BY — here that's power_source.

questions.question: Add a new row to gadget_group with group_id 12 and group_label 'Concrete and Masonry'.
questions.solution:
INSERT INTO gadget_group (group_id, group_label)
VALUES (12, 'Concrete and Masonry');
questions.verify: SELECT group_id, group_label FROM gadget_group ORDER BY group_id
questions.explanation: Naming the columns before VALUES is the safer form — it keeps working if the table later gains a column. This question is graded on the data afterwards, on a throwaway copy of the database.

questions.question: Every gas-powered tool is going up in price. Raise daily_fee by exactly 2.00 for every gadget whose power_source is 'Gas', and leave every other gadget alone.
questions.hint: UPDATE tablename SET column = expression WHERE …; The new value can be built from the old one.
questions.verify: SELECT gadget_id, power_source, daily_fee FROM gadget ORDER BY gadget_id
questions.explanation: SET daily_fee = daily_fee + 2.00 reads the old value and writes the new one. Leaving off the WHERE would raise the price of all 45 gadgets — the classic mistake with UPDATE.

questions.question: Remove every course_result row whose score_pct is below 60.
questions.explanation: DELETE removes rows but leaves the table itself in place — that is the difference between DELETE (DML) and DROP TABLE (DDL).

questions.question: Write a CREATE TABLE statement for a table called workshop with: a workshop_id integer primary key; a workshop_name that is text and may not be null; a seat_limit integer that defaults to 12; and a branch_id integer that is a foreign key referencing branch(branch_id).
questions.modelAnswer:
CREATE TABLE workshop (
  workshop_id   INTEGER,
  workshop_name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL,
  seat_limit    INTEGER DEFAULT 12,
  branch_id     INTEGER,
  PRIMARY KEY (workshop_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (branch_id) REFERENCES branch(branch_id)
);
rubric: Used CREATE TABLE with the table name and a parenthesised column list
Gave workshop_name a NOT NULL constraint
Gave seat_limit a DEFAULT of 12
Declared workshop_id as the PRIMARY KEY
Declared branch_id as a FOREIGN KEY referencing branch(branch_id)
questions.explanation: Constraints can be written inline on the column or as separate clauses at the end — both are accepted. What matters is that all four constraints are present.

questions.question: In your own words: what is the difference between an INNER JOIN and a LEFT OUTER JOIN, and when would you reach for the outer one?
questions.modelAnswer:
An inner join returns only the rows that match on the common value in both tables. Anything unmatched on either side disappears from the result.

A left outer join returns all of those matched rows, plus every remaining row from the left-hand table, filling the right-hand columns with nulls where there was no match.

You reach for the outer join when the absence of a match is itself the answer — listing patrons who have never borrowed anything, or branches that hold no units. With an inner join those rows would simply vanish, and you would never see them.
rubric: Said an inner join keeps only matching rows
Said a left outer join also keeps the unmatched rows from the left table
Mentioned that the missing side comes back as nulls
Gave a case where you need the outer join — finding rows with no match
questions.explanation: The giveaway phrasing in a question is "never", "no", or "without any" — those all mean you need to keep unmatched rows.

questions.question: A classmate writes: SELECT branch_id, count(*) FROM unit WHERE count(*) > 20 GROUP BY branch_id; It fails. Explain why, and write the corrected statement.
questions.modelAnswer:
WHERE filters individual rows, and it runs before the rows have been collected into groups — so at that point count(*) does not exist yet and cannot be tested. Aggregates have to be filtered with HAVING, which runs after GROUP BY has formed the groups.

Corrected:

SELECT branch_id, count(*)
FROM unit
GROUP BY branch_id
HAVING count(*) > 20;
rubric: Explained that WHERE filters rows before grouping, so the aggregate does not exist yet
Said the aggregate condition belongs in HAVING instead
Wrote a corrected statement with GROUP BY before HAVING
Kept the clauses in the right order: SELECT, FROM, GROUP BY, HAVING
questions.explanation: Clause order is fixed: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY — and that order is close to the order in which they take effect.

questions.question: In Crow's Foot notation, what does the crow's foot itself indicate?
questions.explanation: The crow's foot is the "many" symbol. Whatever sits beside it — a bar or a circle — sets the minimum.

questions.question:
An ERD shows an entity box laid out like this:

    row 1:  P1 | **P2**   (bold, underlined)
    row 2:  P3 | *P4*     (italic)
    row 3:  P5 (one or more fields)

Slot P5 is annotated "one or more fields". What goes there?
options: Nothing — P5 is always left blank
questions.explanation: After the primary key and any foreign keys, the rest of the box lists the ordinary descriptive attributes.

questions.question: Business rule: "A PATRON can place many HOLDS, but each HOLD is placed by exactly one PATRON." What is the cardinality between PATRON and HOLD?
questions.explanation: One patron relates to many holds, each hold to one patron — a textbook 1:M.

questions.question:
Business rules: "A MEMBER may or may not have submitted any REVIEWS yet. A MEMBER can submit many REVIEWS. Every REVIEW is submitted by exactly one MEMBER."

Legend: A = crow's foot; B = bar + crow's foot; C = circle + crow's foot; D = single bar; E = double bar; F = circle + bar.

Which connector belongs on the REVIEW end of the line?
questions.explanation: A member might have zero reviews (optional, so a circle) but could have many (crow's foot) — connector C.

questions.question: A single sentence such as "a DEPOT stores many CRATES" is enough to place connectors on both ends of the relationship line.
questions.explanation: Relationships are bidirectional. That sentence fixes the CRATE end only; you still need to know how many depots a crate can belong to, and whether either side is optional.

questions.question: Business rule: "One MENTOR guides many APPRENTICEs, but an APPRENTICE is guided by only one MENTOR." The foreign key mentor_id would be placed in the ______ table.
questions.explanation: APPRENTICE is on the many side, so it holds mentor_id as its foreign key.

questions.question: Why can't a 1:M relationship be recorded by putting the foreign key on the "one" side instead?
options: It can — either side works equally well
Because that single column could hold only one of the many related key values
Because foreign keys may never appear in the same table as a primary key
Because the DBMS would reject the CREATE TABLE
questions.explanation: One column holds one value. To point at many children you'd have to stuff several key values into one field, which breaks the atomic attribute rule.

questions.question: After resolving an M:N between VOLUNTEER and SHIFT with a bridge entity SIGNUP, how many relationship lines does the ERD show, and of what type?
options: Two 1:M lines — VOLUNTEER to SIGNUP, and SHIFT to SIGNUP
questions.explanation: The bridge sits on the many side of both relationships, so a single M:N becomes two 1:M relationships.

questions.question: In a bridge entity resolving an M:N relationship, what is true of the two key columns it holds?
options: They are foreign keys individually, and together they form the composite primary key
They are primary keys individually and cannot be foreign keys
They must both be surrogate keys
Only one of them may be a foreign key
questions.explanation: Each points back to its parent table as a foreign key; the pair together identifies the row.

questions.question: Two entities can be joined by more than one relationship line on the same ERD.
questions.explanation: They often are. STEWARD and BRANCH can carry both "works at" (1:M) and "manages" (1:1) — two different relationships between the same pair.

questions.question: A relationship in which an entity is related to other instances of ITSELF — a steward who supervises other stewards — is called:
questions.explanation: A recursive or unary relationship. In SQL you read it with a self-join, giving the table two aliases.

questions.question: In a recursive supervisor relationship, why is the supervisor_id of the most senior person null?
options: Because that person has no supervisor, and the participation is optional
Because null is required by entity integrity
Because the column is a primary key
questions.explanation: Optional participation at that end. Referential integrity permits a foreign key to be null; it only forbids a value that matches nothing.

questions.question: Which phrase in a business rule tells you the MINIMUM cardinality rather than the maximum?
questions.explanation: "May or may not" sets the minimum to zero. "Can have many" and "has only one" both describe the maximum.

questions.question: In Crow's Foot notation, the two symbols at one end of a relationship line express the minimum and ______ cardinality for that end.
questions.explanation: Minimum then maximum, reading from the outside in.

questions.question: A design shows CUSTOMER, INVOICE, INVOICE_ITEM and PRODUCT. Which describes INVOICE_ITEM's role?
options: It is a bridge entity: each row is one line of an invoice, linking that invoice to one product
It is a duplicate of INVOICE and should be removed
It is the parent of INVOICE
questions.explanation: An invoice can list many products and a product can appear on many invoices — M:N, resolved by the detail-line table between them.

questions.question: When a business rule mentions no attributes at all, the ERD still needs the primary and foreign key fields.
questions.explanation: The keys are what carry the relationships, so they belong on the diagram even when the rules describe no other fields.

questions.question: Explain, in your own words, the difference between cardinality and participation, and say how each is drawn in Crow's Foot notation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Cardinality is about how many — whether one instance of an entity can be related to one other instance or to many. It sets the maximum, and it is drawn with the inner symbol: a bar for one, a crow's foot for many.

Participation is about whether the relationship is required at all — whether an instance must take part or may stand alone. It sets the minimum, and it is drawn with the outer symbol: a bar for mandatory (at least one), a circle for optional (zero).

So a line ending in circle + crow's foot means optional participation with a maximum of many — "zero or many" — while a double bar means mandatory participation with a maximum of one: "one and only one".
rubric: Said cardinality is the maximum — one versus many
Said participation is the minimum — optional (zero) versus mandatory
Linked the circle to optional/zero and the bar to one
Linked the crow's foot to many
questions.explanation: Every connector on the legend is just these two ideas stacked: minimum on the outside, maximum on the inside.

questions.question: Normalization assigns attributes to tables based on:
questions.explanation: Determination — that is, functional dependence. Attributes travel to the table whose key determines them.

questions.question: Which requirement is NOT part of 1NF?
options: There are no repeating groups in the table
All attributes are dependent on the primary key
questions.explanation: Eliminating transitive dependencies is 3NF. 1NF is about tabular format, no repeating groups, and a defined primary key.

questions.question: A table can be in 2NF while still containing a transitive dependency.
questions.explanation: 2NF only removes partial dependencies. Removing transitive dependencies is what takes you to 3NF.

questions.question: A table in 3NF is automatically also in 2NF and 1NF.
questions.explanation: The forms are cumulative — 3NF is defined as 2NF plus no transitive dependencies.

questions.question: In the dependency BOOKING_REF → BOOKING_DATE, match each attribute to its role.

pairs.right: The determinant attribute
The dependent attribute

questions.explanation: The determinant is on the left of the arrow and does the determining; the dependent is on the right.

questions.question: The generalized definition of functional dependence says attribute A determines attribute B if:
options: A and B are in the same table
All rows in the table that agree in value for A also agree in value for B
questions.explanation: Rows agreeing on A must agree on B. This is the version you can actually test against sample data.

questions.question: If attribute B is functionally dependent on composite key A, but NOT on any subset of A, then B is:
questions.explanation: Full functional dependence on a composite key means you need the whole key, not a piece of it.

questions.question: A functional dependence in which the determinant is only PART of the primary key is called a ______ dependency.
questions.explanation: A partial dependency. It can only arise when the primary key is composite — a single-column key has no proper parts.

questions.question: A dependency in which an attribute depends on another NON-key attribute is called a ______ dependency.
questions.explanation: A transitive dependency. It occurs only when functional dependence exists among nonprime attributes.

questions.question: Transitive dependencies are harder to spot than partial ones. Why?
options: They involve the primary key, which is often hidden
They occur among nonprime attributes, so neither side of the dependency is part of the key
They only appear in tables with more than twenty columns
They can only be detected by running a query
questions.explanation: With a partial dependency you can scan the parts of the key. A transitive dependency hides between two ordinary attributes, so you have to reason about the data's meaning.

questions.question:
Consider CATERING_ORDER (booking_ref, booking_date, client_no, client_name, client_city, dish_code, dish_name, dish_style, dish_price, portions), where the primary key is booking_ref + dish_code.

What kind of dependency is dish_code → dish_name?
options: A full functional dependency on the primary key
questions.explanation: dish_code is only half of the composite key, so anything it determines on its own is partially dependent.

questions.question: In CATERING_ORDER (PK = booking_ref + dish_code), what kind of dependency is (booking_ref, dish_code) → portions?
options: A full functional dependency on the whole primary key
questions.explanation: How many portions of a dish were ordered depends on which dish AND which booking — you need the whole key, so it's fully functionally dependent and stays put.

questions.question: In CATERING_ORDER (PK = booking_ref + dish_code), client_no depends on booking_ref, and client_name depends on client_no. What is client_name's relationship to booking_ref?
options: A full functional dependency on the composite key
questions.explanation: booking_ref → client_no → client_name. Because client_no is not a key attribute, that chain is a transitive dependency.

questions.question: In CATERING_ORDER, which set of attributes should move into a DISH table when you convert to 2NF?
questions.explanation: Everything determined by dish_code alone travels with it, and dish_code becomes the new table's primary key. portions stays behind — it needs both halves of the key.

questions.question: After splitting CATERING_ORDER into 2NF, one table is BOOKING (booking_ref, booking_date, client_no, client_name, client_city). Why is this still not in 3NF?
options: client_name and client_city depend on client_no, which is not the primary key
questions.explanation: A transitive dependency. Splitting out CLIENT (client_no, client_name, client_city) and leaving client_no behind as a foreign key gets you to 3NF.

questions.question: SEMINAR_ROSTER (seminar_code, seminar_title, room_code, room_capacity, attendee_id, attendee_name, grade) has primary key seminar_code + attendee_id. Which is a TRANSITIVE dependency?
questions.explanation: room_code is not part of the key, and it determines room_capacity — a dependency between two nonprime attributes. The first two options are partial dependencies; the last is a proper full dependency.

questions.question: In SEMINAR_ROSTER (PK = seminar_code + attendee_id), which attribute is fully functionally dependent on the whole key?
questions.explanation: A grade belongs to one attendee in one seminar, so it needs both halves. Everything else depends on just one part, or on a nonprime attribute.

questions.question: A repeating group in a table looks like:
options: Several columns holding the same kind of fact — phone1, phone2, phone3 — or several values crammed into one cell
Two rows with the same primary key
A foreign key that appears twice
A column with the same value in every row
questions.explanation: Either shape breaks 1NF. Both are fixed the same way: move the repeating fact into its own table, one row per value.

questions.question: A TRAIL_PERMIT table stores a column trail_codes containing values like 'RID-2, LKE-7, SUM-1'. Which normal form does this violate, and how is it fixed?
options: 1NF — split the repeating group into its own table, one row per trail
It violates nothing; the values are comma-separated for efficiency
questions.explanation: Multiple values in one cell is a repeating group, which breaks 1NF and the atomic attribute rule. It is the same mistake as stuffing several key values into one foreign key field.

questions.question: ______ deliberately produces a lower normal form, increasing performance at the cost of greater data redundancy.
questions.explanation: Denormalization. It is a considered trade-off, not an accident.

questions.question: Why might a designer choose to denormalize?
options: To increase performance, accepting greater redundancy in return
Because 3NF is not a valid design
To remove the need for primary keys
questions.explanation: More tables mean more I/O operations and more processing logic to join them, so there is a real cost to normalizing.

questions.question: A table is in 3NF but one of its determinants is not a candidate key. Which normal form does it fail?
questions.explanation: BCNF requires every determinant to be a candidate key. It is a special case of 3NF.

questions.question: Match each problem to the normal form that fixes it.

pairs.left: A cell holding several values at once
pairs.right: 1NF

pairs.left: An attribute determined by half of a composite key
pairs.right: 2NF

pairs.left: An attribute determined by another non-key attribute
pairs.right: 3NF

pairs.left: A determinant that is not a candidate key
pairs.right: BCNF

questions.explanation: Reading a dependency diagram left to right, these are the four faults you're hunting for, in the order you fix them.

questions.question: Normalization is the whole of database design.
questions.explanation: Normalization is important, but only part of the design process.

questions.question: Explain the practical difference between a partial dependency and a transitive dependency: how you spot each one, and which anomaly each one causes.
questions.modelAnswer:
A partial dependency is a non-key attribute determined by only PART of a composite primary key. You spot it by covering up half the key and asking whether the attribute is still determined — if dish_code alone tells you dish_price, dish_price is partially dependent. It can only exist when the key is composite. The anomaly: the dish's price is repeated on every order line for that dish, so changing it means changing many rows, and a dish nobody has ordered yet cannot be recorded at all.

A transitive dependency is a non-key attribute determined by ANOTHER non-key attribute. You spot it by looking for a chain among ordinary attributes — booking_ref determines client_no, and client_no determines client_name. Neither side of client_no → client_name is part of the key. The anomaly: the client's details are repeated on every booking they make, and deleting their last booking erases the client entirely.

Both are fixed the same way: move the determinant and everything it determines into a new table, and leave the determinant behind as a foreign key.
rubric: Defined partial dependency as determined by part of a composite key
Defined transitive dependency as determined by another non-key attribute
Noted that a partial dependency requires a composite primary key
Named a concrete anomaly caused by each
Said both are fixed by splitting the determinant into its own table with a foreign key left behind
questions.explanation: If you can state the fix in one sentence — new table keyed on the determinant, foreign key left behind — you can normalize anything you're given.

questions.question: A classmate says: "My table has a single-column primary key, so I skipped 2NF and went straight to checking 3NF." Are they right? Explain.
questions.modelAnswer:
Yes, they are right, and for the correct reason. A partial dependency means an attribute is determined by part of the primary key. A single-column primary key has no proper parts, so no partial dependency can exist. Any table in 1NF with a simple key is therefore already in 2NF, and going straight to hunting for transitive dependencies is legitimate.

What they must not skip is the 3NF check itself. A single-column key gives no protection at all against a chain like booking_ref → client_no → client_name, which is exactly the kind of dependency 3NF exists to remove.
rubric: Agreed that they are right
Explained that a partial dependency needs part of a composite key, and a one-column key has no parts
Concluded that such a table is automatically in 2NF
Warned that the 3NF check still matters, because transitive dependencies are unaffected
questions.explanation: Worth internalizing: composite key means look for partial dependencies; any key at all means look for transitive ones.
